parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the row for gel in Table 8.1 - you are given two properties, density and speed of sound, and impedance is the property that combines how heavy the medium is with how fast sound moves through it.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what specific acoustic impedance means**
Think of $Z$ as telling you how much resistance a medium offers to sound passing through. A denser medium with faster sound speed has a larger $Z$. It is found by multiplying the two together.

Step 2: **Multiply for gel**
For gel, $\rho = 1200 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and $c = 1400 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$Z = \rho c = 1200 \times 1400$$
$$Z = 1,680,000 = 1.68 \times 10^{6} \text{ kg m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$$
This matches the value to be shown.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: rearrangement rho = Z/c and c = Z/rho
hints: Hint 1: You now know impedance links density and speed together, so if one of them is missing you can work backwards from the impedance value already in the table.
Hint 2: For air divide $Z$ by $c$ to get density, and for tissue divide $Z$ by $\rho$ to get speed, then round each to three significant figures with correct units.
parts.proper_answer: density of air $= 1.29 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, speed of sound in tissue $= 1540 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the same link backwards**
You know:
$$Z = \rho c$$
So for air where $\rho$ is missing:
$$\rho = \frac{Z}{c}$$
And for tissue where $c$ is missing:
$$c = \frac{Z}{\rho}$$

Step 2: **Calculate the two missing values**
For air, $Z = 440 \text{ kg m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$ and $c = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$\rho = \frac{440}{340} = 1.29 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$$
For tissue, $Z = 1.68 \times 10^{6} \text{ kg m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$ and $\rho = 1090 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$:
$$c = \frac{1.68 \times 10^{6}}{1090} = 1.54 \times 10^{3} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 1540 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Both to three significant figures.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what controls reflection at a boundary - it is the mismatch or difference between the $Z$ values on the two sides, air ($440$) and tissue ($1.68 \times 10^{6}$).
Hint 2: Substitute into $\alpha = (Z_{1}-Z_{2})^{2}/(Z_{1}+Z_{2})^{2}$ using $Z_{1}=440$ and $Z_{2}=1.68 \times 10^{6}$ and evaluate.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the reflection rule**
When ultrasound meets a boundary, the fraction of intensity reflected depends only on the two impedances:
$$\alpha = \frac{(Z_{1} - Z_{2})^{2}}{(Z_{1} + Z_{2})^{2}}$$
A large difference gives $\alpha$ close to 1, meaning almost total reflection.

Step 2: **Insert air and tissue values**
$Z_{air} = 440$, $Z_{tissue} = 1.68 \times 10^{6}$:
$$\alpha = \frac{(1.68 \times 10^{6} - 440)^{2}}{(1.68 \times 10^{6} + 440)^{2}}$$
$$\alpha \approx \frac{(1.67956 \times 10^{6})^{2}}{(1.68044 \times 10^{6})^{2}} \approx 0.999$$
So almost all the intensity is reflected.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Compare the $Z$ values for gel and tissue from part (a) - notice how close they are and think what that means for the numerator $(Z_{1}-Z_{2})^{2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the matched impedances**
Both gel and tissue have:
$$Z \approx 1.68 \times 10^{6} \text{ kg m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$$
So:
$$\alpha = \frac{(Z_{gel} - Z_{tissue})^{2}}{(Z_{gel} + Z_{tissue})^{2}} = \frac{0}{(sum)^{2}} = 0$$
There is essentially no reflection at a gel-tissue boundary.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Look back at your two values of $\alpha$ in (b) - one is almost 1 and the other is almost 0, so think what each one says about reflected versus transmitted intensity.
Hint 2: Link this to a real scan: the probe is outside the skin, so without gel there is an air gap, while with gel the air is replaced - explain which case lets ultrasound enter the body.
parts.proper_answer: Without gel, $\alpha \approx 0.999$ so almost all incident ultrasound is reflected at the air-skin boundary and almost none enters the tissue. With gel, $\alpha \approx 0$ so almost all incident ultrasound is transmitted into the tissue.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Interpret the air-tissue result**
$\alpha \approx 0.999$ means about 99.9 percent of the incident intensity is reflected. If only air is between the probe and skin, the ultrasound bounces off the skin and almost nothing is transmitted in to be reflected by internal structures.

Step 2: **Interpret the gel-tissue result**
$\alpha \approx 0$ means almost zero reflection and almost 100 percent transmission. Gel has almost the same $Z$ as tissue, so it removes the air gap and matches the impedances. This lets the ultrasound pass into the body and back out to the probe, giving a strong signal for imaging.
